summary:
An opinion piece by Tom Florsheim Jr. (CEO, Weyco Group) and Adam Goodman (CEO, Goodmans Interior Structures), originally published in Fortune and syndicated via Allwork.Space, argues that employers are an underused lever for increasing voter turnout, and that doing so requires no partisan stance.

The authors contrast expensive campaign and PAC spending, which randomized trials suggest lifts turnout by only a point or two, with new academic research linking LinkedIn employment records to voter files across 30 million workers at 377,000 employers. Researchers at Michigan, Harvard, Columbia and Maryland also tracked 8 million job changers to control for selection bias, finding workers who moved to a higher-scoring employer became 3.5 percentage points more likely to vote, rising to 5.8 points for a move from the 25th to the 75th percentile employer. Effects hold across political affiliations.

The argument: workplaces shape behaviour because people spend most of their time there, and employers control formal levers such as Election Day scheduling and leave policy. Most corporate leaders do not know where their firm sits on this distribution and should find out.

Practical examples are given. Weyco runs a communications calendar prompting employees to make a voting plan, flagging early voting, and reminding them the week before and on Election Day; it offers paid leave for voting or poll work, arranges rides, and hosts voter registration assistance on site. Goodmans partners with Power the Polls to recruit poll workers, offering a stipend and a paid day off. Resources cited include a Wisconsin Business Leaders for Democracy toolkit and Leadership Now Project.

The piece notes nearly half of local election jurisdictions struggled to recruit enough poll workers for the 2024 general election (U.S. Election Assistance Commission), naming shortages in Milwaukee, Kenosha, Maricopa County, Ohio, North Carolina and Nevada. It closes by arguing voting is habit-forming, spreads to households, matters most in primaries, and supports business-friendly stability.
